deep.reconstruction:
Context: in the 1983-84 notes on systems (arrangements) of pseudo-lines, Grothendieck is trying to build a 2-dimensional cell complex, a surface \tilde X, that encodes how 'stable' pseudo-lines D change under elementary moves. Each stable pseudo-line D carries a polygon (disc) \Delta_D. Its boundary edges are the 'arcs of transition' for D (moves across a vertex), the 'arcs of specialization', and the antipodes of these. On the previous page he glued these discs, together with Möbius bands built from two rectangles, using parallel transport.

On this page he first asks whether the first construction (gluing the polygons edge to edge) is really just a quotient of the second. The second would be the same polygons, with doubled centre points, glued in pairs along edges. The justification is that the \Delta_D come in antipodal pairs, and the antipodal map is compatible with the identifications, so passing to the quotient by the antipodal involution gives the expected cellular edges.

He then reinterprets the new edges as the edges of a graph. Its vertices are the pseudo-lines. For two adjacent pseudo-lines D, D' there are now two arrows, a_D: D -> D' and a_{D'}: D' -> D. Each carries an orientation, and the two directions are deliberately 'de-identified'.

Next he restates the polygonal structure: transition arcs (strict transversals) for D, i.e. edges of \Delta_D, together with specialization arcs and their antipodes, arranged into polygons in the usual way. The resulting surface \tilde X maps to X, by an immersion according to the next page. The inverse image of the 1-skeleton X_1 gives a cellular decomposition associated with the faces of (\tilde X, K).

Finally he starts a purely combinatorial description, continued on the next page:
1) A graph \Gamma. Vertices are the stable pseudo-lines D. Oriented edges are pairs (D,a), with a a transition or specialization arc for D, or the antipode of one. The opposite of (D,a) is (D',a'), where D' is obtained by flipping D and a' by parallel transport.
2) A polygonal structure, i.e. a cyclic order of the oriented edges leaving each vertex.
3) 'Transport of orientations', i.e. a ±1 twist on each edge.

Together, (1)-(3) are exactly the data of a graph cellularly embedded in a possibly non-orientable closed surface: a rotation system with edge signatures, i.e. a twisted ribbon graph, the non-orientable version of the 'cartes' of the Esquisse. The surface is recovered by gluing polygons along these data. The next page records that with one choice of data (3) the expected 'circuits' do not appear, while with parallel transport they do but the natural map \tilde X -> X is lost.
errors: The text is openly tentative ('non ??', 'sauf erreur'). The claim that the first surface is a quotient of the second by the antipodal involution is asserted without checking that the involution is free on the cells, apart from the doubled centre points it introduces.

The page does not settle whether the two orientation-transport choices give the same surface. The next page shows they do not give the desired 'circuits' simultaneously with a map to X, so the construction here is unresolved.

ideas.what: Encoding a cellular surface by a graph with an opposite-edge involution, cyclic order at vertices, and orientation transport (edge signs) on oriented edges
ideas.modern_name: Signed rotation system / twisted ribbon graph / generalized map (combinatorial map of a possibly non-orientable surface)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Heffter, Edmonds, Ringel, Gross–Tucker; Lins (gems); Grothendieck's 'cartes' in the Esquisse (orientable case)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984), section on cartes / dessins, orientable case; the twisted variant with orientation transport is not there as far as I know

ideas.what: A 2-complex/surface whose vertices are stable pseudo-lines of an arrangement, whose edges are elementary moves (transition/specialization arcs and antipodes), and whose 2-cells are polygons \Delta_D, viewed as a quotient by the antipodal involution of the projective setting
ideas.modern_name: Flip/mutation complex of pseudo-line arrangements; cellular structures related to Ringel's flip graph and higher Bruhat orders B(n,2)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ringel (1956, flip connectivity); Manin–Schechtman (1989, higher Bruhat orders); Bokowski, Felsner and others on flip graphs

ideas.what: Quotienting a double (antipodal) polygonal complex to obtain the cellular edges, with doubled centre points
ideas.modern_name: Orientation double cover / quotient by a free involution in the projective-plane setting

missed.claim: Grothendieck sets up a combinatorial-map encoding of a surface built from local polygons attached to pseudo-lines and glued along elementary moves (flips), with explicit orientation-transport data allowing non-orientable pieces (Möbius bands). He is trying to realize such complexes over X. This anticipates treating flip complexes of pseudo-line arrangements as surfaces described by twisted ribbon graphs, which does not seem to be pursued in the oriented-matroid literature.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a potential bridge between the 'cartes'/dessins formalism of the Esquisse and the topology of pseudo-line arrangements and higher Bruhat orders. It is of modest interest, since the construction is unfinished and its target is not clearly identified.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is exploratory scaffolding. Its main content is setting up a standard encoding of a surface by a signed rotation system (twisted ribbon graph) for a complex built from pseudo-lines and flips. The application to arrangements is unpublished and mildly interesting, but the page is unresolved and largely routine.
transcription_corrections: 'munie[?] de X par une involution' should most likely read 's'envoie dans X par une immersion' (or similar), consistent with the next page's 'pas une immersion' and 'application naturelle \tilde X -> X'.
The surface is written \tilde X (a script X with tilde), not \mathcal X.

'cellules polaires[?], habituelles des fs[?] p.d. (CW[?])' is uncertain; more plausibly it refers to the usual cellular structure ('cartes ... habituelles') of the pseudo-line system, i.e. a CW structure.
'(Wagner[?] cellulaires)' is uncertain; the image suggests a short underlined parenthetical like '(arêtes cellulaires)'.
'dont les sommets sont les pseudo-droites' should be completed as 'pseudo-droites stables' per the later description of vertices.
'(de l'arête a vers b')' / '(de l'arête b vers a)': the labels are partly illegible and should be flagged as uncertain.
